Does a trade deficit mean that one country sells fewer dollars worth of goods than another? If so, I don't see a problem with that. What's the problem?
What's wrong with having a trade deficit?

A trade deficit occurs when a country imports more than it exports.

That means it's spending more money on the global market than it's making off the global market.

That means it's pushing money out of it's own economy in exchange for goods, and depleting the money supply, without making up the shortfall in exports.

That means, in order to keep the domestic money supply stable, it has to print more money than it otherwise would if there was no trade deficit.

That means that there's a ton more currency floating around in the world that the government has no control over, and if suddenly it all comes back at once, it's going to cause some monetary havoc.

Trade deficits are bad, mmm'kay?

There's nothing fundamentally "wrong" with a deficit, especially in the short term. But remember the longer it goes on the more wealth is moving from the buyer to the producer.

Think on micro terms... If I have money and you have stuff... I give you money for the stuff... Eventually you have the money and I don't.

Food... We need it, but we always need more. If we run out of money and can't buy more, that's a problem.

Machinery... Like a tractor used to work the land and produce food we can eat and sell. Good use of money because it provides long term value (a capital asset)

This is why the reports on trade deficits usually also talk about 'durable goods' as they offset the deficit.

Also... Printing money when there's a shortage... That's a primary cause of inflation (more cash means each dollar buys less, more supply & less demand).

Some inflation is OK but if the deficit goes on too long, the inflation will eat up the econom. e.g. last year I could buy a loaf of bread for a dollar, 6 months ago, 5 dollars, today $10... Did my salary go up 10 times?

This is the reality in Venezuela today. Trade deficit caused by bad policy and poor investment in the infrastructure, I suggest you go read how bad the inflation is there today.

Trade deficits are not necessarily bad. Remember that fiat currency is representative of productive capacity, not intrinsic value. E.g. if a country is vastly more productive than its trading partners, it will be able to buy more internationally than it sells internationally at no harm to itself. E.g. I buy bottles of scotch, but it's unlikely anyone in Scotland will ever buy anything from me. And I dont care, because even if I lit that currency on fire instead of engaging in international trade, I would still be vastly more productive than most Scotsmen.

Trade deficits become an issue when a country's currency isn't in demand in the international market for its potential purchasing power (Zimbabwe and Venezuela come to mind), which can lead to sudden inflation as all of that currency comes home at once.
It's not a big deal if you're a highly productive nation, but if you're an economic basket case it can lead to inflation because other countries will decide they need to cash in now or they'll never be able to get anything from you.
